article.title: Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Hitachi Energy is aware of multiple vulnerabilities that affect MicroSCADA X SYS600 product versions listed in this document. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to carry out various attacks on the product. Please refer to the Recommended Immediate Actions for information about the mitigation/remediation. The following versions of Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 Product are affected: MicroSCADA X SYS600 vers:MicroSCADA_X_SYS600/ CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 Hitachi Energy MicroSCADA X SYS600 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Neutralization of Formula Elements in a CSV File, Incorrect Implementation of Authentication Algorithm Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Energy Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Switzerland Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-9852 A CSV injection vulnerability exists in SYS600. Injected malicious formulas can add or modify data to the spreadsheet, insert links, exfiltrate data, and in some cases, depending on how the user has their environment configured, execute malicious code on the user’s machine. To exploit this issue attackers would need a way to create arbitrary log messages. This could be achieved through normal functionality via SCIL scripts, a log injection vulnerability, or via the SYS600 broker. This vulnerability affects all Windows users regardless of their privilege level who can run the Notify service and export the log. Read More 1 Affected Product MicroSCADA X SYS600 versions 1

Such practices include that process control systems are physically protected from direct access by unauthorized personnel, have no direct connections to the Internet, and are separated from other networks by means of a firewall system that has a minimal number of ports exposed, and others that have to be evaluated case by case. Process control systems should not be used for Internet surfing, instant messaging, or receiving e-mails. Portable computers and removable storage media should be carefully scanned for viruses before they are connected to a control system. Proper password policies and processes should be followed. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-9852 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-9852 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-9852, CVE-2026-9853, CVE-2026-9854; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-9852.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-9852 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-9852/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-9852 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-9852')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-9852, CVE-2026-9853, CVE-2026-9854; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.hitachienergy.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('2.1.7.5') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-9852, CVE-2026-9853, CVE-2026-9854; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: Thermo Fisher Torrent Suite Software
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to read arbitrary files on the Torrent Server. The following versions of Thermo Fisher Torrent Suite Software are affected: Torrent Suite Software CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 6.5 Thermo Fisher Torrent Suite Software 1 Vulnerability Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Healthcare and Public Health Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-107777 The affected product is vulnerable to a path traversal, which could allow an authenticated attacker to read arbitrary files on the Torrent Server that are accessible to the web service account. Read More 1 Affected Product Thermo Fisher Torrent Suite Software: Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fix Thermo Fisher has fixed the vulnerability and recommends users update Torrent Suite Software to version 5.22 or later. Mitigation For more information, refer to Thermo Fisher's Security bulletin. article.title: Inductive Automation Ignition Software
article.summary: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an authenticated low-level user to escalate their privileges to a higher level. The following versions of Inductive Automation Ignition Software are affected: Ignition >=8.1.0| Ignition >=8.3.0| CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Inductive Automation Ignition 1 Vulnerability Incorrect Authorization Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-92817 The Ignition Perspective module does not properly validate session privileges when determining Designer-level access. An authenticated user with access to a Vision project could provide their valid Vision session identifier and gain Designer-level privileges. An attacker could exploit these elevated privileges to execute arbitrary code in the context of the Ignition Gateway process. Read More 2 Affected Products Inductive Automation Ignition: >=8.1.0| Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Inductive Automation released version 8.3.9 in August 2025 and version 8.1.55 in September 2026 to address this issue. Users are recommended to update to the newest version available. Mitigation For more information, see the publication at the Inductive Automation Trust Center. Inductive Automation Ignition: >=8.3.0| Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Inductive Automation released vers
article.raw_text: Inductive Automation Ignition Software View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an authenticated low-level user to escalate their privileges to a higher level. The following versions of Inductive Automation Ignition Software are affected: Ignition >=8.1.0| Ignition >=8.3.0| CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.8 Inductive Automation Ignition 1 Vulnerability Incorrect Authorization Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Information Technology Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-92817 The Ignition Perspective module does not properly validate session privileges when determining Designer-level access. An authenticated user with access to a Vision project could provide their valid Vision session identifier and gain Designer-level privileges. An attacker could exploit these elevated privileges to execute arbitrary code in the context of the Ignition Gateway process. Read More 2 Affected Products Inductive Automation Ignition: >=8.1.0| Product Status: known_affected Remediations Mitigation Inductive Automation released version 8.3.9 in August 2025 and version 8.1.55 in September 2026 to address this issue. Users are recommended to update to the newest version available. Mitigation For more information, see the publication at the Inductive Automation Trust Center. Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 8.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 8.7 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Tim Hemingway reported this vulnerability to Inductive Automation. Legal Notice and Terms of Use This product is provided subject to this Notification ( https://www.cisa.gov/notification ) and this Privacy & Use policy ( https://www.cisa.gov/privacy-policy ). Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as virtual private networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting this vulnerability has been reported to CISA at this time. hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-92817 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-92817 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-92817; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-92817.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-92817 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-92817/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-92817 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-92817')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-92817; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.cisa.gov') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-92817; vectors: phishing, exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds Four Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-0322 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Code Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-76519 Cisco Secure Email Gateway Relative Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2026-105133 Ahsay AhsayCBS Improper Authentication Vulnerability CVE-2026-105134 Ahsay AhsayCBS Command Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue

article.title: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th)
article.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
article.raw_text: Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 14th) [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] [This is a Guest Diary by Zachary Norwood, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Crypto mining malware has been active and spreading across the internet for quite some time now. Moreover, the DShield honeypot picked up a worm that self-propagates through a plethora of means. One of them is stealing SSH keys after it gains access to a system. Furthermore, it also leverages a rootkit to maintain access to infected systems. One would hope that threat actors would have moved on past this worm by now. However, due to its rudimentary design and its effectiveness, they have had no reason to move on. A malicious binary was uploaded and executed on the DShield honeypot, and that is where a copy of the Panchan worm was obtained. It is written with Golang, and it is a peer-to-peer botnet. Moreover, this worm was first identified in 2022. Many vendors recognize this worm now as seen below. VirusTotal Clamscan Therefore, a system with security controls such as egress filtering, ingress filtering, access control lists, continuous monitoring, and passwordless authentication will prevent this worm from taking root. However, many systems are insecure and unpatched. This is why this worm is still propagating across the internet. The strings captured from the binary below show how simple it is to find its command-and-control channel and the functions that it consists of. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Command and Control Channel Panchan Functions These captures clearly show the source files that the Panchan worm consists of. To dig deeper into what this binary can do, a network simulator was used. Moreover, the specific network simulator that was used was FakeNet-NG with Wireshark to intercept the network traffic. These tools were used to identify what URL it was reaching out to once it was installed on a system. FakeNet-NG is a tool developed by the Mandiant FLARE team for dynamic network analysis. This tool simulates legitimate network traffic, allowing an analyst to identify how the malware interacts with the network and if it is communicating with an external server. This specific strain of this worm was using a discord channel as a command-and-control server. This was identified by capturing and dissecting the network traffic that was generated by the worm interacting with the FakeNet-NG network. FAKENET-NG Wireshark Capture Panchan, the peer-to-peer crypto mining worm, is a threat to any organization who has internet facing servers. This worm is mainly a threat to insecure systems, and opening SSH to a public network needs to be done in a secure way. Fail2Ban is a service that scans log files for repeated failed login attempts. This service then blocks that IP address by updating the system’s firewall rule. Fail2Ban is another control that should be put in place with a public facing SSH port. Services like SSH should have multi-factor authentication, and an access control list. The access control list should include specific IP addresses or a jump box. Disabling root login with SSH is another essential security control that needs to be implemented. With SSH, public and private key pairs are another option for authentication. This will then create the capability to disable password authentication for the SSH service preventing brute force attacks. However, these key pairs are often created and forgotten about. This is a security concern, and SSH private keys are something that this worm is designed to steal. Once it has stolen a private key, it attempts to pivot to hosts in the running user’s SSH known_hosts file. A simple mitigation to protect the data within the known_hosts file is to use the HashKnownHosts option within a systems SSH configuration. Furthermore, it is best to mitigate long lived credentials and SSH key stealing by leveraging tools likeHashiCorp Vault to sign SSH certificates with short expirations. This ensures that reusing a key becomes highly impractical or even impossible. The user will authenticate to Vault with their credentials then they send their SSH public key to Vault for signing, and finally Vault then signs the SSH key. Then it returns the SSH certificate to the user. This certificate can be used to log in to any host configured to trust the Vault CA. Leveraging such infrastructure will also allow an organization to disable password authentication entirely for services like SSH. Furthermore, leveraging something as simple as syslog to pull logs and using commands such as grep to find privilege escalation activities, software installation, software removal, and access to ports such as SSH will allow an analyst to identify this activity. However, this does not scale well. Therefore, leveraging a SIEM to gather and parse this data is a much more effective solution. Next, all traffic entering and exiting from both the trusted and untrusted networks needs to pass through at least one firewall. Preferably, also having an intrusion detection or prevention system right after the public facing firewall in the trusted zone. Typical indicators of compromise for this worm include multiple failed authentication attempts via SSH, unusual resource usage on infected systems, and processes that cannot be killed by any means. This worm also creates hidden directories in the running users home directory or folders like /tmp. Often, these directories have names that are strings that have high amounts of entropy. For this strain of this worm, servers reaching out to services like Discord on a regular basis is another indicator of compromise that an analyst can look for. In conclusion, denying by default and allowing by exception is a vital strategy for systems facing untrusted networks. These same techniques that were discussed above can be used to protect critical public facing infrastructure from threat actors. article.raw_text: Ivanti Connect Secure zero-day exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-104935) Overview On October 13, 2026, Ivanti published a security advisory for CVE-2026-104935 , a high-severity authentication bypass by spoofing ( CWE-290 ) affecting Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS). The vulnerability has a CVSSv3.0 score of 8.6 and allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands. Ivanti reports that exploitation in the wild has already occurred prior to disclosure, affecting a limited number of customers. This indicates that exploitation has been occurring as a zero-day vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirms exploitation in the wild, and added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on the same day as the vendor's public disclosure. The digital forensics firm Volexity has published a detailed blog post describing the threat actor activity, which was detected in early October 2026. Volexity notes that in addition to leveraging CVE-2026-104935 as a zero-day, the threat actor also leveraged an as-yet unpatched privilege escalation vulnerability which Ivanti are planning to patch at a later date. According to the vendor, a portion of the vulnerability was initially discovered through its product security program and patched in the July 2026 release of 25.1.3.0 . Exploitation occurred while Ivanti was working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions. Ivanti Connect Secure is a popular enterprise VPN solution and naturally sits on the edge of a corporate environment. The product has a history of being targeted by attackers, with zero-day exploitation of other vulnerabilities occurring back in both 2024 and 2025 . Given the confirmed exploitation, the ability to execute commands without authentication, along with the history of the product, Rapid7 recommends that organizations running affected versions apply the appropriate update on an emergency basis outside of normal patching cycles. Mitigation guidance Vendor-supplied updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-104935. Ivanti lists the following affected and resolved versions: Ivanti Connect Secure affected versions Resolved versions 25.1.1.1 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.1.2 25.1.2.2 and prior in the applicable code line 25.1.3.0 , 25.1.3.1 22.8R2.4 and prior in the applicable code line 22.8R2.5 Note that the vendor advisory confirms that versions 22.7.x and below are unaffected. At the time of the advisory, Ivanti states that reliable indicators of compromise are not available, however Volexity have published several here . Rapid7 strongly recommends looking for signs of compromise even after the patch has been applied. Customers who suspect exploitation should follow the vendor's recovery steps . For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the vendor's security advisory . Rapid7 customers Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-104935 with a vulnerability check expected to be available in the October 14 content release. Updates October 13, 2026 : Initial publication.

hypotheses.title: Initial access via CVE-2026-80466 affecting the affected product/service
hypotheses.statement: A threat actor has attempted to obtain initial access to our environment by exploiting CVE-2026-80466 in the affected product/service within the last 30 days.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'initial_access_cve' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to the affected product
objectives.falsification_criterion: If zero internet-facing assets run a vulnerable build of the affected product, the external-exploitation hypothesis is disproven for CVE-2026-80466.
objectives.suggested_query: asset_inventory | where product == 'the affected product' and exposure == 'internet' and version in (vulnerable_versions)

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge
objectives.falsification_criterion: If WAF / firewall / IDS show no exploit-signature hits for CVE-2026-80466 in the last 30 days, in-the-wild exploitation against us is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: edge_logs | where signature contains 'CVE' or uri matches /exploit-pattern-for-CVE-2026-80466/ | summarize count() by src_ip, dst_host

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2026-80466 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.
objectives.suggested_query: patch_state | where kb in (fixes_for('CVE-2026-80466')) | summarize coverage = avg(installed) by host_role

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep
objectives.falsification_criterion: If a sweep of webroots and IIS/Apache process trees finds no anomalous children (cmd, powershell, /bin/sh) on the affected product hosts, post-exploit foothold is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where parent in ('w3wp.exe','httpd','nginx','java') and child in ('cmd.exe','powershell.exe','/bin/sh','/bin/bash')

objectives.title: Honeypot / canary check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If exposed canary instances of the same product show no probing or exploitation telemetry, opportunistic mass-exploitation against the org is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: canary_events | where product == '<product>' | where event_type in ('probe','exploit') | summarize by src_ip

hypotheses.title: Outbound C2 beaconing to reported infrastructure
hypotheses.statement: Hosts in the estate are beaconing to the command-and-control infrastructure reported in this article (domains, IPs, TLS fingerprints, or RMM tooling).
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'c2_beacon' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: DNS resolution sweep for published C2 domains
objectives.falsification_criterion: If recursive DNS logs show zero resolutions for the IOC domains in the last 90 days, active beaconing is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: dns | where query in ('www.wago.com') | summarize count() by client_ip

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: egress | where dst_ip in ('the published C2 IPs') | summarize bytes_out = sum(bytes_sent) by src_ip

objectives.title: Beacon periodicity / jitter analysis
objectives.falsification_criterion: If beacon-style periodic outbound connections (low jitter, small payloads) to uncategorised destinations are absent, covert C2 is unlikely.
objectives.suggested_query: conn | summarize stddev_interval = stdev(diff(ts)), count() by src_ip, dst_host | where count() > 50 and stddev_interval < 5s

objectives.title: TLS / JA3 fingerprint pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If JA3/JA3S fingerprints associated with the reported family are absent in TLS telemetry, encrypted C2 attribution is weakened.
objectives.suggested_query: tls | where ja3 in (ti_lookup('family','ja3')) | summarize by src_ip, sni

objectives.title: Remote-monitoring tooling abuse check
objectives.falsification_criterion: If unmanaged AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installs are absent, RMM-based C2 is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: process | where name in ('anydesk.exe','teamviewer.exe','screenconnect.exe','atera*.exe') and signer != 'corp_managed'

hypotheses.title: Identity compromise of privileged users
hypotheses.statement: Privileged identities have been compromised through phishing, MFA fatigue, help-desk social engineering, or OAuth illicit-consent grants.
hypotheses.rationale: Archetype 'identity_compromise' selected based on CVEs cited: CVE-2026-80466, CVE-2026-88850; vectors: exploit, vpn-edge.

objectives.title: Impossible-travel / atypical sign-ins
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra ID / Okta risky-sign-in detections show no impossible-travel hits on privileged identities, account compromise is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: signin | where risk_level in ('high','medium') and user in (privileged_users) | summarize by country, ip

objectives.title: MFA-fatigue / push-bombing
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MFA telemetry shows no bursts of denied pushes followed by a successful one for the same user, MFA-fatigue compromise is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: mfa | summarize denies = countif(result=='deny'), accepts = countif(result=='accept') by user, bin(ts,1h) | where denies > 5 and accepts > 0

objectives.title: Help-desk social-engineering pivot
objectives.falsification_criterion: If ticketing / call-recording shows no recent password-reset or MFA-reset requests for privileged users without proper verification, help-desk vector is unsupported.
objectives.suggested_query: tickets | where action in ('password_reset','mfa_reset') and target in (privileged_users) | join (verifications) on ticket_id

objectives.title: OAuth illicit-consent grants
objectives.falsification_criterion: If Entra/Workspace audit logs show no recently consented third-party apps with high-impact scopes, OAuth abuse is disproven.
objectives.suggested_query: audit | where action == 'Consent to application' and scopes contains 'Mail.Read' or 'files.read.all'

article.title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
article.summary: CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. article.raw_text: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog , based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-96652 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96654 Plex Media Server Improper Neutralization of Encoded URI Schemes in a Web Page Vulnerability CVE-2026-96655 Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability CVE-2026-96656 Plex Media Server External Control of File Name or Path Vulnerability CVE-2026-106931 EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition OS Command Injection Vulnerability CVE-2026-110936 Siemens Software Center Uncontrolled Search Path Element Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities . CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria . Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form . Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

objectives.title: Inventory exposure to Fortinet FortiOS

objectives.title: Hunt for exploit attempts at the edge

objectives.title: Patch-status correlation
objectives.falsification_criterion: If MDM / patch-management shows 100% deployment of the CVE-2025-61624 fix across exposed hosts, the hypothesis is disproven by remediation.

objectives.title: Post-exploit web-shell sweep

objectives.title: Egress connections to published C2 IPs
objectives.falsification_criterion: If proxy / firewall egress logs show no connections to the IOC IPs or matching ASNs, network-level C2 is unsupported.

article.title: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers
article.summary: Adversaries are turning the tools businesses trust into delivery mechanisms for malicious activity. Cisco Talos observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms over the past year, exploiting the built-in trust of collaboration, file-sharing, payment and other services to reach their targets.
article.raw_text: Parasitizing trust: How legitimate infrastructure becomes a delivery pipeline for attackers Adversaries are turning the tools businesses trust into delivery mechanisms for malicious activity. Cisco Talos observed abuse of more than 25 legitimate platforms over the past year, exploiting the built-in trust of collaboration, file-sharing, payment and other services to reach their targets. Legitimate infrastructure has become a powerful delivery mechanism for attackers, carrying the inherent trust they once had to build. As Cisco Talos explored in our previous research on weaponizing software-as-a-service (SaaS) notification pipelines , these platforms are increasingly repurposed as proxies for malicious intent. Talos has since tracked a significant acceleration in this trend, observing abuse across more than 25 distinct legitimate platforms in the past year. The abused infrastructure included collaboration, productivity, file-sharing, survey, payment and AI-related platforms. This demonstrates that attackers are not limiting themselves to traditional phishing infrastructure or lookalike domains. Instead, they are systematically subverting the very tools businesses trust. Order notification abuse Talos recently analyzed two order notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines. Together, these campaigns accounted for roughly 1,400 messages observed by Talos. The malicious element was not the outer sender identity, like a simple forged sender or lookalike domain. It was the content of the legitimate order notification workflow rendered. The suspicious content appeared inside the notification itself, in fields that would normally contain shipping information. The attacker’s objective was to use a trusted retail pipeline to create urgency around a high-value purchase and push the recipient toward an attacker-controlled phone number. In the first campaign, the message appeared as a Staples order confirmation from "support@orders.staples.com” with the subject line, “Here’s your Staples order #9939818875. Thanks for shopping with us.” The body displayed a plausible purchase for an Apple iPad, including order number, delivery timing, pricing, billing information and standard Staples footer content. The suspicious element was embedded in the order details: “Helpline 806 283 7712,” “Order Confirmed,” and the Staples corporate address appeared in fields normally associated with shipping or billing information. Figure 1. Staples order notification The structure of the message matters. The attacker was not trying to persuade the user to click a crude phishing link. Instead, the message created the impression that an expensive order had already been placed and that the fastest way to resolve it was to call the embedded “helpline.” The desired user action was a phone call. Once the victim moved from email to voice, the attacker could continue the scam through social engineering, payment manipulation, credential theft, or remote assistance fraud. The headers reinforced the trust problem. The Staples message showed DKIM alignment for “orders.staples.com” and DMARC passed for the visible Staples domain. The message also passed through forwarding and re-encapsulation paths, including Proton Mail, Microsoft 365, and downstream enterprise mail infrastructure. These hops complicate provenance analysis, but they do not change the core issue: Authentication helped establish that the outer message was credible, while offering no assurance that the phone number or transaction context was legitimate. The second campaign used the same pattern in a Dell order received notification. The message was sent from “Dell | Order Received ” with the subject line, “We have your order | Dell Purchase ID: 2009829958247.” The body presented a purchase for Microsoft Project Standard 2024, totaling $736.09. As with the Staples example, the suspicious content appeared in transaction fields. The “Ship To” and “Bill To” sections included “Confirmed Order,” “Helpline 808 232 6397,” and “Call Our Sales Team”. The Dell message used the same psychological lever: an unexpected high-value purchase, a legitimate-looking order template, and a phone number positioned as the path to resolution. The attacker did not need the recipient to trust a new domain or unfamiliar brand. The message borrowed credibility from Dell’s order pipeline and redirected the recipient toward attacker-controlled contact information. Authentication results showed DKIM passing for Dell-related infrastructure and DMARC passing for “order.dell.com”. As with the Staples sample, forwarding artifacts and SRS-style return paths appeared as the message moved through Microsoft and enterprise mail infrastructure. But the malicious intent did not live in an obviously forged sender. It lived inside the rendered order content. Figure 2. Dell order notification These campaigns illustrate the same trust-boundary failure described in our earlier research on platform-as-a-proxy (PaaP) abuse. In those cases, attackers placed malicious content into SaaS fields that trusted platforms later rendered into notifications. Here, the same concept appears in commerce infrastructure, in the retailer’s order pipeline. The attacker supplies the intent, while the trusted system performs the delivery. From a defensive perspective, sender authentication is necessary, but it is not sufficient. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC help answer whether a message came from expected infrastructure. However, they do not answer whether the transaction was legitimate, whether the rendered fields make business sense, or whether the user is being pushed toward an attacker-controlled action. Order notifications should be treated as sensitive content. Any field reflected into a transactional message — shipping name, billing name, address line, company name, order note, support field, or fulfillment instruction — can become a delivery vehicle if it is not validated before rendering. Retailers and security teams should correlate order notification content with account history, payment state, shipping context, and known support channels. Transactional templates should reject or flag unexpected phone numbers, URLs, urgency language, and support instructions when they appear in fields where they do not belong. In both campaigns, the wrapper was legitimate enough to inherit trust. The payload was attacker-influenced. That distinction is the center of this attack class. The abuse of commerce pipelines is merely one manifestation of a broader, systemic vulnerability. Whether the attacker initiates a fake purchase or a fraudulent account sign-up, the root cause remains the same: Platforms are implicitly trusting data that enters their systems from untrusted sources, only to render that data into high-reputation, automated notifications. This same mechanism of reflection — where input is echoed back into an email to a third party — is the engine behind an evolution in list bombing, moving the attack from simple denial-of-service to a sophisticated vehicle for content delivery. List bombing: From inbox disruption to content delivery List bombing is an abuse technique in which attackers submit a victim’s email address to numerous legitimate registration, subscription or notification workflows, flooding the inbox with automated messages. While this vector is traditionally viewed as a denial-of-service or distraction tactic designed to bury critical alerts in a flood of junk, Talos has observed a subset of cases where this behavior is being repurposed as a delivery vehicle for malicious content. This abuse occurs when an attacker identifies public-facing registration, profile, or project-naming forms that lack sufficient input validation. By inputting a "hostile string" — such as a cryptocurrency-themed lure — into fields intended for a name, company, or title, the attacker forces the platform to treat this data as legitimate user information. When the service reflexively incorporates this input into its automated welcome, verification, or notification templates, the system acts as an unintended carrier, delivering the attacker’s content inside a high-reputation, system-generated email that can pass standard authentication checks. The attacker’s objective in these cases is to bypass the security perimeter by laundering their malicious content through the brand reputation of a trusted service provider. While this is not yet a broad industry shift, it represents a calculated abuse of a platform's trust boundary. By embedding their lure in an automated notification, the adversary ensures that the message arrives with the appearance of administrative legitimacy, significantly increasing the likelihood that the recipient will trust the content. The goal is to reach the target's inbox with enough platform authority that the message may be evaluated as routine notification traffic rather than attacker-controlled content. Figure 3. Registration field reflection Beyond the risk to the individual recipient, this vector creates a significant brand liability. When a service provider’s infrastructure is used to broadcast fraudulent content, the resulting user complaints and bounce-backs can degrade the platform's own sender reputation, potentially triggering blocklisting that impacts their legitimate business communications. Bounce abuse: When delivery reports carry the lure The final vector moves the abuse pattern into the mail system itself. Instead of relying on a retailer, SaaS platform, or registration workflow to generate the message, the attacker attempts to make a delivery status workflow carry attacker-controlled content. Bounces, formally known as delivery status notifications (DSNs) or non-delivery reports (NDRs), are generated when a message cannot be delivered. Under normal conditions, a mail system sends the delivery report back to the original SMTP envelope sender. Depending on the implementation, that report may include the original headers, portions of the message body, URLs, attachments, or an encapsulated copy of the failed message. That returned content creates the abuse opportunity. In one example Talos observed, a mail delivery system notification carried a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure. The administrative wrapper made the message look like routine mail-system noise, while the nested content asked the recipient to engage with what appeared to be a file transfer workflow. The attacker’s goal was to make the phishing lure feel less like an unsolicited external message and more like part of a technical delivery failure that required review. Users are conditioned to view system errors as benign and are far more likely to engage with an "administrative" fix than a suspicious, standalone phishing email. Figure 4. Bounce carrying a file-sharing lure There are several ways this kind of message can reach a victim. In opportunistic backscatter, an attacker sends mail using the victim’s address as the forged envelope sender. If an intermediate system accepts the message and later fails to deliver it, the resulting DSN may be sent back to the forged sender. If the DSN includes enough of the original message, the bounce itself can carry the lure. A second possibility is intentional bounce abuse, where the attacker uses an authenticated, compromised, or otherwise controllable sending context to trigger a delivery failure that returns attacker-influenced content. This differs from an outright forged NDR, where the attacker simply fabricates the bounce message and sends it directly. From the recipient’s mailbox, however, these cases can look similar: A delivery-failure wrapper contains content the attacker wants the user to trust. This distinction matters for defenders. A DSN’s administrative appearance does not validate the content inside it. The outer message may be a legitimate delivery report, while the returned or encapsulated content may still contain a phishing link, credential harvesting page, malicious attachment, or social engineering prompt. The content-trust gap: A defensive imperative Across these vectors, the defensive failure is consistent: Trusted infrastructure is being treated as a shortcut for trusted content. Sender authentication remains essential. SPF, DKIM, DMARC, reputation, and infrastructure analysis help determine whether a message came from an expected source. But these controls do not answer a separate and increasingly important question: What was that trusted system instructed to carry? Order notifications, registration workflows and delivery reports all create opportunities for attacker-influenced content to appear inside messages that users and security tools are conditioned to trust. In the Staples and Dell campaigns, the suspicious content was a phone number placed into transactional fields. In list bombing and registration abuse, the lure can appear inside reflected account or profile data. In bounce abuse, the malicious content may sit inside returned message data or a nested MIME object. Defending against this requires content-aware validation at multiple points in the delivery chain. Platform owners should treat any user-controlled value rendered into an email template as untrusted data. Fields used for names, addresses, company names, project titles, order notes or support instructions should be validated before storage and again before rendering. Phone numbers, URLs, markup, line breaks, and urgent support language should be rejected or flagged when they appear in fields where they do not belong. Security gateways should inspect the fully rendered message, not only the sender or template. That includes HTML, text, URLs, redirects, attachments, personalization fields, and nested MIME content. For transactional email, defenders should also evaluate whether the message content aligns with the workflow that produced it. An order notification containing unexpected support numbers, cancellation instructions, or high-urgency language should be treated differently from a routine receipt. For delivery reports, recursive MIME inspection is especially important. Gateways should parse DSN containers, extract returned messages or message fragments, and apply normal phishing, malware, and URL analysis to the nested content. A bounce should explain a delivery failure, not provide a blind path for untrusted payloads. The broader lesson is that attackers are no longer only exploiting technical vulnerabilities in infrastructure. They are exploiting the assumptions built into business processes. When legitimate systems render attacker-influenced data into trusted notifications, the result can pass authentication checks and still deliver malicious intent. Defenders should therefore treat sender trust and content trust as separate but complementary signals. The wrapper can explain where a message came from. It cannot prove that the payload is safe. Acknowledgments Special thanks to Eric Peterson, Dev Shah, and Adam Katz for their professional guidance and input during the development of this research.

article.title: CISA Urges Patching Critical Vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support
article.summary: CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 , affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05 . Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. Or
article.raw_text: CISA Urges Patching Critical Vulnerability in BeyondTrust Remote Support CISA is aware of critical authentication bypass vulnerability CVE-2026-102764 , affecting BeyondTrust Remote Support (formerly Bomgar) versions 26.2.3 and earlier. Patches are available for supported versions (24.3.1 and later); organizations using older versions must upgrade first. Cyber threat actors are actively exploiting the vulnerability to gain initial access, then establishing persistence, escalating privileges, and moving laterally. CISA added CVE-2026-102764 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Oct. 16, 2026. CISA urges organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances to immediately take the following actions: Apply the BT26-05-RS patch, as outlined in BeyondTrust’s Security Advisory BT26-05 . Organizations on a self-hosted Remote Support version older than 24.3.1 will need to upgrade to a newer version to apply the patch. Organizations using BeyondTrust-hosted (SaaS) Remote Support deployments have already been patched. Review BeyondTrust’s blog ARMORY CASTLE and BT26-05: What Security Teams Need to Know for detailed information on the vulnerability and recommended response and mitigation actions. Limit external access to the Remote Support appliance to the services needed to support users and customers. Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted networks. Review BeyondTrust’s B Series Appliance on-premises security for additional guidance on securing network connectivity for self-hosted Remote Support appliances. Organizations with affected self-hosted Remote Support appliances should conduct network and memory forensics to identify evidence of potential compromise. If your organization suspects a compromise, CISA recommends taking the following actions: Isolate any suspected or confirmed compromised appliances. Collect a snapshot of virtual appliances or forensic image for physical appliances to conduct future forensics, immediately forward appliance syslog and session events to the SIEM, and collect any additional logs, such as web application firewall, reverse-proxy, or perimeter firewall logs for the exposure window. Consult BeyondTrust’s Syslog guide for additional information on forwarding appliance logs and session events. Conduct network and forensic investigations for evidence of compromise. Additionally, hunt for indicators of threat actor activity, including unrecognized privileged or administrative sessions, unrecognized script files, unexpected gaps in logs or log forwarding, and unauthorized account, permission, or session-policy changes. Consult CISA’s Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk to assist with prioritizing vulnerability remediation. Rebuild from a known-good state and apply the BT26-05-RS patch. Then rotate every credential the appliance stored or injected, revoke all active support sessions, and review new multifactor authentication registrations on privileged accounts. CISA urges organizations to review the BeyondTrust security advisory and resources noted above and apply necessary updates. CISA also recommends reviewing Mandiant’s blog, ARMORY CASTLE Exploits BeyondTrust , for additional hunt and isolation guidance and detections. article.title: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers
article.summary: The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like?
article.raw_text: There's only so much code: the rise in vulnerability numbers The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? And what does the future look like? Frontier AI models (like Mythos) are rapidly mining decades of technical debt across ubiquitous legacy libraries, driving monthly Microsoft Patch Tuesday vulnerability advisories up more than tenfold (reaching 1,415 this month). This volume is overwhelming open-source maintainers and putting pressure on the traditional 90-day coordinated disclosure model. Despite a 105% year-over-year surge in CVEs, Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) grew by only 37%, and only 3 of September's 975 Microsoft advisories saw in-the-wild exploitation, demonstrating that the vast majority of AI-discovered bugs are not practically exploited. We may be able to take new-bug-class vulnerability spikes as evidence that these vulnerabilities will eventually level off and decline, once the historical code backlog is remediated and AI verification is embedded directly into new development pipelines. With attackers able to parse patches faster via AI, defenders cannot cover for all possible threats. Organizations should continue to build robust defense-in-depth. Prioritize high-exploitability flaws in their specific environments, implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models into their software build chains. The September Microsoft Tuesday release included 975 vulnerability advisories. This month, 1,415 vulnerabilities were just dropped. Compared to a pre-June average of 100 a month, that increase is staggering. Where did they come from? As of April, frontier models came onto the scene more fine-tuned than ever toward vulnerability detection, particularly with the introduction of Mythos. The deluge brings a lot of questions: If these numbers are real, why hasn’t the internet collapsed? Are these vulnerabilities a new breed, and if not, why didn’t analysts find them in code that is sometimes decades old? Is the coordinated disclosure model still relevant in an era of this kind of speed? How in the world do defenders deal with those numbers? Should we go home, kiss our spouses, and prepare for the end? The answer to many of these questions boils down to this: The majority of these vulnerabilities are coming from repositories of old code from large-profile products and systems; and disclosure does not equal weaponization. Where is it from? AI is chewing through a backlog of technical debt in libraries and tools used as the dependable, best-practice lynchpins of so many environments. These models have a new perspective, an ability to "think" without some of the hangups or assumptions of human defenders, and they are thorough in listing those vulnerabilities. Entrenched older tools have always been prime targets because of their predictability; attackers know those tools and all their secrets, and they know what is likely to be present in a network with them. Multi-exploit attacks can be deployed with little variability. Pre-Mythos threat actors exploited log4j ( CVE-2021-44228 ) to immense success. The library was ubiquitous, included in nearly every environment, but not a component that got cataloged in visibility scans. A combination of scale and low visibility meant defenders were blindsided, scrambling to find out if they even used the log4j library before starting to concoct a mitigation plan. Talos has ongoing relationships with some of the largest technical vendors (such as the Microsoft Active Protections Process ( MAPP ) agreement). Organizations share additional information—detection guidance or maybe a POC — for vulnerabilities that are most likely to be exploited, to enable Talos to provide adequate coverage when the advisories are announced. "Microsoft believes it is important for us to provide detection content, based on their guidance," as Yves Younan, Director of Talos Vulnerability Discovery, Detection, and Testing, says. Talos has needed to invest more resources to get coverage in on time for critical vendors like Microsoft to keep up with notifications coming in fast and often on staggered or out-of-band timelines. For larger vendors, the pressure is handleable for now. However, open-source projects are getting flooded. Some projects have a trusted group that can combine to tackle patches, and some share with the full community for immediate assistance, but it is up to the project. The internet runs on open-source work. The pace of discovery presents a challenge for the traditional coordinated disclosure system vulnerability hunters have been using for years, and some are calling it into question. Security vulnerabilities should be reported, to enable an informed defender base and regular patching, and vendors responsible for vulnerable code need time to create coverage. A timed disclosure model where notifications are sent to a vendor, who then has a set period of time (typically 90 days) to provide coverage before the disclosure is released publicly, has created a more secure online environment for decades. Now, many practitioners are releasing advisories publicly without a disclosure period beforehand. The reasoning is that if one AI can find a weakness, any other could, so the vulnerability is already, effectively, released. This conversation is actively changing expectations around vulnerability disclosure, and guidance is in flux. Will it stay this high? No one knows the future, but we can always look to the past for insight. Numbers of vulnerabilities jump drastically when a new bug class is identified, as their possibilities are explored to the fullest. Then the discoveries plateau and drop off. When format string vulnerabilities were discovered as a new bug class in 2000, the initial influx of discoveries ramped up and up, until reaching a peak in 2005 and then slowly declining over the next couple of years. Format string vulnerabilities are still discovered, but they are a smaller overall fraction of the number of CVEs discovered in a year. Theoretically, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery could go the same way. While frontier models have not discovered a new vulnerability class, they are more efficient at discovering known types of software vulnerabilities. Given that a lot of vital software has a long history of code releases, there’s plenty of code to mine for weaknesses. But there’s only so much code… right? Old and commonly used tools are often under the highest scrutiny, lending them one kind of safety: Because of their popularity, utility, and stability, when popular tools have vulnerabilities, they are discovered fast and patched promptly. As the historical backlog of essential systems is turned over by AI, vulnerabilities will be found and patched. New code will ideally be run through AI bug-checkers that will prevent new vulnerabilities from being introduced. The rate of new vulns should level off and drop accordingly. There are some caveats. In the past, as vulnerability disclosures increased through coordinated disclosures, we saw increased adoption of mitigations. Exploitation became significantly harder. Attackers often need to chain together 3 or more vulnerabilities to successfully exploit a system. However, more awareness of vulnerabilities often leads to more exploitation. Attackers often use vendor patches meant to protect customers to discover where vulnerabilities might exist. The frequency of patching has delayed human attackers via parsing bottlenecks, but AI can eliminate that problem. Are the numbers the real issue? The volume is certainly up. Fresh as this blog is being finished, the October Patch Tuesday dropped almost 500 more than last month. With refinement, any vulnerability could become a link to a path of effect. But... not all vulnerabilities are exploitable. Some are wildly impractical for attacker use. In fact, the percent of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEVs) is vastly smaller than the found vulnerabilities. Of the 975 vulnerabilities Microsoft reported in September, there were only three in-the-wild exploits detected. When viewed by percentage, vulnerabilities versus KEVs tell a different and perhaps reassuring story. Compared with the same period last year, additions to the known-exploited vulnerability list increased by 37%, while published CVEs increased by 105%. However, we wouldn't necessarily expect those figures to grow in proportion. Adversaries only need enough useful vulnerabilities to compromise their targets, and the same vulnerabilities can be reused against many organizations. The KEV count tracks distinct vulnerabilities known to be exploited, not the number of attacks or successful compromises. AI helps ingest code, advisory reports, and attack surfaces with inhuman speed, but it cannot currently make judgment calls about the value of a weakness. For defenders, the question remains the same: Which vulnerabilities provide a viable path into their environment, and how do you close those paths? What do we do now? The undeniable danger here is in exploitation time going down rapidly, while the vulnerabilities that could become exploits is still going up. The biggest hurdle for a defender is determining what is a real vulnerability for their environment, and what is not. Different defenders have different forms of control depending on their role. For those who are writing code, the new standard validation chain should include AI evaluation by models at least as up to date as those being used to hunt for vulnerabilities. It is relatively cheap to run new code through AI, but very expensive to run a cumbersome backlog of old code through. Bite it off in chunks. For those whose role involves keeping the tools ready: Upgrade ASAP. Don't stop there. For Cisco customers, implement LiveProtect to mitigate vulnerabilities between advisory release day and patching, to give time for that patching. Do this for everything you own. Move beyond static domain blocking and implement behavioral detection that alerts on anomalous traffic patterns directed toward automation platforms. Hone your focus to the vulnerabilities with the highest exploitability in your environment. KEVs are far less common among the sea of advisories, and their numbers have not risen proportionally with the AI-assisted deluge. Focus on building defense-in-depth. Employ multiple protection systems, to cover for delays in patching. Implement interim mitigations (such as LiveProtect), create custom IPS/Snort triggers to block pre-patched traffic using SnortML, deploy behavioral anomaly detection, and integrate current AI evaluation models in software build chains. Dive deeper into this conversation with the latest TTP interview with Yves Younan and vulnerability researcher Bella Fusari. For more numbers and advice for defenders: Don't swing at everything Threat Source Newsleter: Discovery ≠ Exploitation
